h1: Brewing with unmalted Indian wheat from the local flour mill
title: Brewing With Unmalted Indian Wheat | Craft Beer School
desc: How to brew with unmalted wheat from an Indian flour mill: choosing kernels or dalia, how much to use, mashing for enzymes and avoiding a stuck mash.
teaser: That sack of wheat from the local chakki can make a proper witbier, if you mill it right and give it enough malt to work with.
standfirst: Wheat is everywhere in India and costs a fraction of imported wheat malt. Unmalted wheat is also traditional in Belgian witbier. Here is how homebrewers use it without ending up with wallpaper paste in the mash tun.
sections:
Malted wheat has been steeped, sprouted and dried, which develops enzymes and breaks down part of the grain's structure. Unmalted wheat is simply the raw grain. It brings starch and protein but no useful enzymes of its own. Its starch sits locked in a tougher matrix.

Raw wheat gives a slightly sharper, grainier, more bready flavour than malted wheat and lots of haze-forming protein. That is exactly what Belgian witbier wants. Traditional witbier recipes use a large share of unmalted wheat. Our witbier guide covers the style. Our guide to wheat malt in brewing covers the malted version.

• Whole wheat kernels (gehun). The best choice. Mill them coarsely yourself or at the shop.
  • Dalia (broken wheat). Already cracked, convenient and widely available. Choose a coarse grade.
  • Atta (whole wheat flour). Avoid it as the main form. Fine flour turns to a sticky paste and can stop your lauter completely.
  • Sooji and maida. Semolina and refined flour. Also not ideal, for the same reason.

Buy clean, food-grade grain without added oil or flavouring. Most Indian wheat is bread wheat, which works well.

Raw wheat needs enzymes from the rest of the grist. Base malts such as pilsner or pale ale malt have plenty to spare. As a working range:

  • 10% to 20% adds body, haze and foam to pale ales and saisons.
  • 30% to 50% is witbier territory, with the rest pale base malt and often a little oats.

Above about half the grist, conversion and lautering both get harder. Stick to well-modified base malt for the rest.

Wheat starch gelatinises at temperatures close to normal mash temperatures, unlike rice or maize, which usually need a separate cereal cook. That means you can add cracked wheat straight to the mash. Our guide to rice and maize adjuncts explains the cereal cook for those grains.

Many homebrewers simply single-infusion mash at about 65 to 67 °C. Some add a rest around 45 to 50 °C for 15 to 20 minutes to help break down the gums (beta-glucans and pentosans) that make raw wheat sticky. Give the main rest a full 60 to 75 minutes and check conversion with an iodine test if you are unsure. A long, gentle mash helps.

Raw wheat has no husk and plenty of sticky gums. Together they make a dense, slow-draining mash. To keep it moving:

  1. Crack the wheat coarsely. You want broken kernels, not flour.
  2. Add rice hulls, around 5% of grist weight, to rebuild the filter bed.
  3. Use a slightly thinner mash.
  4. Recirculate slowly and never open the valve all the way at the start.
  5. Brew in a bag if you struggle. The bag does the filtering.

Wheat kernels are small and hard. In a roller mill set for barley, many slip through barely touched. Mill wheat separately at a tighter gap, or run it through twice. Dalia saves you this step, which is one reason many Indian homebrewers start with it. Do not ask a flour chakki to grind it. Even their coarsest setting is usually too fine.

A beer with a lot of raw wheat tastes slightly tart, grainy and bready, with a soft, almost creamy mouthfeel. It will be hazy. That haze is permanent, because it comes from wheat protein and starch rather than yeast. Do not try to cold crash or fine it bright. A witbier should look like lemonade.

Foam is usually excellent, since wheat proteins support a dense, long-lasting head. If your beer is cloudy with a starchy, doughy taste, conversion was incomplete. Next time mash longer, check with iodine and make sure the base malt share is high enough.

For a 20 litre batch at around 1.048: 2.2 kg pilsner malt (50%), 1.8 kg coarse dalia or cracked wheat (41%), 0.4 kg rolled oats (9%), plus about 200 g rice hulls that do not count towards the grist percentages. Season with a little crushed coriander seed and dried orange peel in the last few minutes of the boil and ferment with a witbier yeast. It is a good first recipe for learning how raw grain behaves.

Raw grains reward brewers who understand what enzymes and gums are doing in the mash, which is why they are a good next step once a basic all-grain brew is going well.
faqs: Can I use atta in beer?
Not as the main form. Fine flour turns into a sticky paste and can block your lauter. Use whole kernels or coarse dalia.
Does unmalted wheat need a cereal cook?
Usually not. Wheat starch gelatinises close to normal mash temperatures, so cracked wheat can go straight into the mash.
How much unmalted wheat can I use?
About 10% to 20% for body and haze in many ales. Use 30% to 50% for witbier, with base malt providing the enzymes.
How do I stop a wheat mash sticking?
Crack the wheat coarsely, add rice hulls, use a slightly thinner mash and recirculate slowly.
